findings.summary: Historian MG Sashibhooshan says Kerala had no restaurant before 1815, with temple ootuppuras feeding only Brahmins and kanjipurakal feeding the poor. Critic CS Venkiteswaran argued the tea shop was the one space where caste or religion did not matter, provided one could pay.
findings.why_interesting: The paying transaction, not any reform rule, is presented as what made the space a caste leveler.

findings.summary: Tea in India was a pushed colonial product: the Indian Tea Association found little Indian market in 1881, a 1903 cess funded marketing, and a 1930s Depression surplus triggered campaigns of free samples and employer tea breaks. Turkey reportedly shows a similar policy-created demand path, later locked in by social venues.
findings.why_interesting: A drink now seen as inseparable from Kerala daily life was reportedly created by state and industry marketing rather than indigenous demand.

findings.summary: Tea shops reportedly bundled a cheap information subscription with a drink: the shop bought one newspaper each morning and it was read aloud to villagers who could not afford their own. George Woodcock (1967) noted over 40 Malayalam papers read and discussed by all classes and castes.
findings.why_interesting: The sustaining product may have been shared news access, with tea as the entry fee.

findings.summary: Communists in the 1920s used tea shops and reading rooms for political education, and K Madhavan called his village tea shop the central office of political activity. Parties thereby used the venues as distribution infrastructure, which gave them a reason to keep them alive (the persistence link is an inference from the note).
findings.why_interesting: Political actors, not just customers, had an incentive to sustain the venue.

findings.summary: No sign bars women from chayakadas, yet women are almost absent from the discussions, and one article argues tea stalls challenged caste but not patriarchy. Yet a tea stall run by Christian women in Kanjirapally was described in the 1890s.
findings.why_interesting: Open-to-anyone-who-pays did not open the space to women, and early women-run stalls challenge the assumption that tea shops were always male-run.

findings.summary: Indian Coffee House outlets were slated to be shut after a mid-1950s policy change, but workers backed by communist leader A. K. Gopalan formed cooperatives, with the first Kerala outlet opening in Thrissur in 1958. Each society is governed by a committee elected from its employees.
findings.why_interesting: A comparable venue type was preserved by worker ownership rather than market or state design.

findings.summary: London coffeehouses (news, conversation, paying customer) drew attempted suppression by Charles II in 1675 over 'false news', and Middle Eastern coffeehouses reportedly faced bans from Cairo clerics, Ottoman and Safavid rulers. The Arabic coffeehouse source carries an unverified-text notice, so the Middle East details are disputed.
findings.why_interesting: The same news-plus-talk venue mechanism repeatedly provoked state anxiety, and the London case reportedly failed to suppress it.

findings.summary: Hotel Brothers in Bharananganam, Kottayam, traces its origins back nearly 140 years and is described as one of Kerala's oldest surviving nadan chayakkadas. Its longevity is attributed to porotta, beef curry and a mixed clientele, not tea.
findings.why_interesting: The oldest surviving example reportedly endures because of food and regulars, which complicates a tea-centered explanation.
